title: The DevOps Engineering Fieldbook
pacingNotes: Treat each week as a 14-hour learning block, not a promise that every unfamiliar setup finishes on schedule. Use the gate weeks to consolidate existing work.

Reserve at least four hours in each gate week for remediation, evidence and handoff. Optional tool installations and public-authentication extensions replace other extensions; they are not extra mandatory work.
If a prerequisite gate fails, repeat its weakest exercise before advancing. Extend the calendar or defer optional breadth rather than marking unproven skills complete.
Keep teaching authentication private or tunneled. A public deployment requires an established identity model, maintained verification tooling and demonstrated application authorization.
Free local practice is the required zero-cloud-bill route. Local acceptance and provider execution are distinct scopes; never claim cloud behavior from a local pass.

weeks.title: Own your Linux environment
weeks.outcome: Find a process, its owner, listening socket, logs, configuration, and resource use without guessing.
weeks.concept: A service is a process with dependencies, permissions, configuration, and a lifecycle. The shell is an observation tool before it is an automation tool.
weeks.focus: Shell navigation and pipes; users and permissions; processes and signals; Git commits, branches and safe reverts.
build: Create a Linux lab and a Git repository with notes, app, tests and evidence directories. Record OS, available RAM and tool versions.
Run a local HTTP server bound to 127.0.0.1; identify its PID, owner and listening port using ps and ss.
Create a branch, introduce a harmless wrong configuration, commit it, then recover using git revert.
weeks.break: Start a second server on the same port. Explain the address-in-use error using socket and process evidence; stop only your lab process.
prove: Locate the correct process and port from a fresh terminal.
Recover your intentional Git mistake while preserving history.
Explain standard output, standard error, exit status and file ownership in your own words.
weeks.deliverable: evidence/week-01.md with commands, observations, repository history and a 5-minute explanation.
weeks.question: What would distinguish a process that never started from one that started but cannot accept traffic?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Follow one request through the network
weeks.outcome: Separate DNS, transport, TLS, HTTP and application failures.
weeks.concept: A successful name lookup does not prove a connection works; a connection does not prove the application is correct.
weeks.focus: IP, ports, CIDR, routes, DNS records and TTL; TCP; TLS identity; HTTP methods and status codes.
build: Draw browser → DNS → connection → TLS → reverse proxy → service → database, marking trust boundaries.
Use curl -v and a DNS lookup tool to observe an HTTPS request to a public documentation site.
Run the lab server on loopback, then compare connection refused, a wrong path and a deliberate application error.
weeks.break: Use an incorrect hostname or local port in a client configuration without modifying your machine's global DNS. Diagnose the failing layer.
prove: Predict the difference between timeout, connection refused, TLS verification error and HTTP 500.
Explain why 0.0.0.0, localhost and a container service name are different.
Explain /24 addressing and a default route using a small example.
weeks.deliverable: An annotated request diagram and four short diagnosis records.
weeks.question: If curl works on the server but fails from your laptop, what would you inspect next and why?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Build a small service you understand
weeks.outcome: Create Taskboard, a deliberately small API that will grow with your operational skills.
weeks.concept: Keep the application understandable so failures reveal infrastructure and delivery lessons rather than unfamiliar business logic.
weeks.focus: HTTP contracts, input validation, configuration through environment variables, structured errors and unit testing.
build: Implement create/list/get/complete task endpoints, initially using in-memory storage. Reject blank titles and unknown task IDs.
Keep task validation in a pure function. Write tests for valid, blank, oversized and malformed inputs.
Add /livez and /version; log a request ID, method, status and duration without logging secrets.
weeks.break: Change a boundary condition so a blank title is accepted. Confirm a test detects it before fixing it.
prove: A fresh checkout runs with documented commands and a recorded dependency lock.
At least one meaningful test fails on an intentional defect and passes after the fix.
API errors are intentional and do not expose stack traces or secret configuration.
weeks.deliverable: Taskboard v0.1 with README, API examples, tests and limitations.
weeks.question: Which tests can run without an HTTP server, and why should they?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Gate 1 · operate a Linux service
weeks.outcome: Start, stop, diagnose and recover your service on a disposable Linux VM.
weeks.concept: Process supervision is a reliability mechanism; repeated restarts are evidence of a problem, not a diagnosis.
weeks.focus: Service users, environment files, systemd units, logs, graceful termination and operational documentation.
build: Run Taskboard as an unprivileged service account in a disposable VM with a documented systemd unit.
Document start, status, journal, stop and restart commands, including where configuration is stored.
Write a small runbook and a clean-machine setup checklist.
weeks.break: Give the lab service a wrong configuration path or an occupied port. Use logs to isolate the cause and recover.
prove: Rebuild from your notes in 60–90 minutes without copying a working VM.
Diagnose the injected fault and explain why the evidence supports your fix.
Show the process does not need root and shuts down cleanly.
weeks.deliverable: Gate 1 evidence, service unit and a reproducible Linux-service runbook.
weeks.question: What happens to in-memory task data after a restart, and what requirement would justify a database?
weeks.cost: Local VM; use a VM if WSL service behavior differs

weeks.title: Package the service with Docker
weeks.outcome: Build and explain an image with a small, explicit runtime surface.
weeks.concept: An image is a packaged filesystem and metadata. A container is an isolated process using that image, not a miniature independent kernel.
weeks.focus: Dockerfile layers, build context, .dockerignore, non-root users, volumes, networking and signals.
build: Containerize Taskboard, excluding Git history, virtual environments and secret files from the build context.
Choose and record a supported base image and its digest. Pin application dependencies and run as an unprivileged user.
Inspect image history and compare build cache behavior after a code-only change versus a dependency change.
weeks.break: Bind the app to localhost inside the container and observe why host port publishing is insufficient. Correct the binding.
prove: The image builds from a clean checkout and runs without source-code mounts.
You can explain every Dockerfile instruction and where mutable data lives.
No credential is copied into a layer; the process handles termination.
weeks.deliverable: Dockerfile, .dockerignore, image digest and build/run notes.
weeks.question: Why can deleting a secret in a later image layer still leave it exposed?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Add PostgreSQL and real integration tests
weeks.outcome: Test the boundary between application code and an actual database.
weeks.concept: Mocks cannot establish SQL, transaction or schema correctness. Integration tests exercise real boundaries in an isolated environment.
weeks.focus: Compose services, database migrations, transactions, persistent volumes, isolated fixtures and readiness.
build: Add PostgreSQL-backed task storage with a migration and a persistent local volume.
Use Compose to start the app and database; avoid publishing the database port unless needed for a local debugging session.
Write integration tests that create a disposable test database or schema and clean up deterministically.
weeks.break: Restart the app and database separately, then use a wrong database hostname. Distinguish persistence from connection configuration.
prove: A created task survives an app restart.
A real-database test detects a schema or transaction defect.
Tests cannot accidentally use the development or future production database.
weeks.deliverable: Compose configuration, migration and isolated integration test suite.
weeks.question: Why is a container being started different from a database being ready?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Prove whole-system behavior
weeks.outcome: Distinguish unit, integration, system, smoke and performance checks by purpose and scope.
weeks.concept: The test level describes what boundary is exercised; test purpose describes what risk is checked.
weeks.focus: Black-box HTTP tests, authentication versus authorization, task ownership, negative cases, isolation and timeouts.
build: Write a system test against the running Compose stack: create → read → complete → read after app restart.

Add a bounded lab-only bearer-token authentication dependency using maintained framework tooling and two synthetic identities. Keep tokens outside Git, enforce task ownership server-side and do not implement a password system. Keep this learning service local or behind a private tunnel.

Add missing/invalid-token, cross-user read/update, malformed-input, missing-record and database-unavailable tests with bounded timeouts. Return no other user's task data and verify that rejected updates do not alter it.
weeks.break: Make the service return HTTP 200 with the wrong response body. Show why checking only the status code misses the defect.
prove: Tests assert user-visible behavior, server-enforced ownership and data consistency.
Failed tests return non-zero exit codes and useful diagnostics.
The two synthetic users cannot read or update each other's tasks; the lab identity mechanism is explicitly unsuitable for an unreviewed public deployment.
weeks.deliverable: Test matrix, authentication/authorization boundary sketch and denied-access evidence.
weeks.question: Can a test have high code coverage and still miss the failure users care about?
weeks.cost: Local; never load-test other people's endpoints

weeks.title: Gate 2 · reproducible local release
weeks.outcome: Release and recover a complete local service from a clean checkout.
weeks.concept: A release is code plus configuration, schema compatibility, evidence and recovery instructions.
weeks.focus: Versioning, reproducible commands, immutable artifacts, backups and release notes.
build: Create explicit commands for unit, integration and system tests; optionally wrap them in Task after understanding the commands.
Tag a release and capture its image digest, dependency versions, migration version and test results.
Back up the lab database and restore it into a second isolated database.
weeks.break: Ship a deliberately incorrect image tag, observe the failure, then restore the known-good artifact without rebuilding it.
prove: A clean checkout starts the stack and all three test levels pass.
Restored data passes a task-count and task-content check.
Your release notes describe rollback limits when the database schema changes.
weeks.deliverable: Taskboard v0.2 release dossier and restore evidence.
weeks.question: Why is rebuilding an old commit weaker recovery evidence than redeploying the exact previous image digest?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Build your first GitLab pipeline
weeks.outcome: Make GitLab execute the same checks you trust locally.
weeks.concept: CI is an executable team agreement about what must be true before a change is accepted.
weeks.focus: Runners, jobs, stages, merge requests, exit codes and JUnit reports.
build: Create a GitLab project and a minimal .gitlab-ci.yml with lint and unit-test jobs.
Run checks on merge requests and use workflow/rules deliberately to avoid duplicate pipelines.
Publish test results with finite artifact retention and make a deliberately failing merge request.
weeks.break: Make a test fail and confirm the pipeline blocks your documented release procedure.
prove: The pipeline executes real commands, not placeholder echo messages.
A failed command fails the job.
You can explain where jobs run and what credentials they can see.
weeks.deliverable: A passing and a failing pipeline linked from your evidence.
weeks.question: Who can modify pipeline code, and what authority does that effectively grant them?
weeks.cost: GitLab quota/runner availability varies; record limits before use

weeks.title: Build once, test and promote
weeks.outcome: Deliver the same artifact through test and staging.
weeks.concept: Caches speed up work; artifacts are declared outputs. Neither is automatically trustworthy because it came from CI.
weeks.focus: needs, artifacts, dependency caches, database services, image registries and digest-based promotion.
build: Add real PostgreSQL integration tests with a separate test database and readiness handling.
Build an image on a suitable isolated runner, push to the registry and record its digest.
Run a system test against that digest, then promote the same digest to a local or disposable staging environment.
weeks.break: Restore a stale dependency cache or omit an artifact dependency. Identify whether the failure is reproducibility or job ordering.
prove: Changing a cache does not change the required correctness outcome.
The digest tested is the digest selected for deployment.
Failures retain useful sanitized logs and test reports.
weeks.deliverable: Pipeline graph, digest trace and test artifacts.
weeks.question: What can go wrong when the deploy job silently rebuilds instead of using the tested image?
weeks.cost: Prefer hosted isolated runners within available quota

weeks.title: Design pipeline trust
weeks.outcome: Explain and limit the credentials and execution privileges a pipeline receives.
weeks.concept: A pipeline runs code. Masking a variable does not prevent malicious job code from using it.
weeks.focus: Protected refs, environment controls, scoped tokens, OIDC identity claims and untrusted merge requests.
build: Draw contributor → runner → registry → deploy-role trust boundaries.
Separate untrusted test jobs from protected deployment jobs and review runner privileges.
Draft narrow OIDC trust conditions for a specific project and protected deployment ref. Implement cloud federation in weeks 20 and 39 after learning cloud IAM.
weeks.break: Use a harmless sentinel variable to verify that an untrusted test path cannot access the deployment secret scope.
prove: No long-lived cloud key is needed in the intended design.
Your design denies the wrong project, audience and ref.
You identify which GitLab controls are available in your tier and document a procedural fallback for paid controls.
weeks.deliverable: Pipeline threat model and a negative-access test record.
weeks.question: What does the cloud verify about an OIDC token before giving the job a role?
weeks.cost: No cloud deployment required

weeks.title: Gate 3 · controlled release and rollback
weeks.outcome: Release through GitLab with observable checks and an exercised recovery path.
weeks.concept: Continuous delivery keeps a change releasable; continuous deployment also automates the production release decision.
weeks.focus: Environments, manual deployment decisions, resource_group, smoke checks and rollback evidence.
build: Add private staging and a protected release path with explicit environment ownership. Keep the core lab local or tunneled; before any public release, replace the teaching tokens with an established identity provider and maintained token-verification library, validating issuer, audience, expiry and task authorization. Treat that public-auth integration as an extension, not permission to expose the toy mechanism.
Serialize deployments to the same environment and reject outdated deployment jobs so an older queued pipeline cannot overwrite a newer approved release; keep pipeline artifacts immutable.
Add post-deploy smoke tests and write a rollback runbook that includes schema-compatibility checks.
weeks.break: Deploy a version with a broken business endpoint but a healthy process. Let the smoke test detect it and roll back.
prove: A failed pre-release check cannot advance through the documented release procedure.
An older queued deployment cannot overwrite a newer approved release; test this separately from simultaneous-job serialization.
You can identify and redeploy the last good digest within a measured lab recovery window.
weeks.deliverable: Taskboard delivery v1, release recording and rollback report.
weeks.question: When is rolling forward safer than rolling back?
weeks.cost: Local staging or explicitly budgeted disposable VM

weeks.title: Learn cloud identity and spending boundaries
weeks.outcome: Understand accounts, regions, availability zones, identities, roles and billing before deploying.
weeks.concept: Cloud APIs can create lasting resources and cost. Identity and ownership are part of the architecture.
weeks.focus: Shared responsibility, MFA, role sessions, least privilege, tagging and budgets.
build: Read the account setup and IAM guidance. Use a dedicated learning account or isolated sandbox and protect privileged access.
Write a proposed monthly ceiling and per-lab inventory; configure budget notifications before paid experiments.
Use short-lived role-based access where available and identify your current account and region before each cloud command.
weeks.break: Attempt a harmless read that your deliberately limited lab role should not allow. Explain the denial.
prove: You can name the identity, account, region and allowed actions of your session.
Budget notifications are configured and you understand they are not a hard spending cap.
Your inventory contains owner, purpose, expiry and cleanup for every planned resource.
weeks.deliverable: Cloud safety worksheet and IAM permission explanation with secrets removed.
weeks.question: What can still cost money after you stop a VM?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Networking and a small EC2 deployment
weeks.outcome: Trace traffic through a VPC, subnet, route table and security group.
weeks.concept: Cloud networking combines address space, routing and policy. A subnet name does not make it private.
weeks.focus: CIDR, public/private reachability, security groups, instance roles, DNS and access paths.
build: Design a minimal single-region network and explicitly mark ingress and egress.

Run Taskboard on one disposable EC2 instance only if the current price fits your lab budget; otherwise rehearse on a VM and mark cloud execution pending. Keep application access private or tunneled while using the teaching authentication mechanism; public access requires an established identity/token-validation model and demonstrated authorization checks.
Restrict administration to your chosen controlled access path and keep the database off public ingress.
weeks.break: Change only the lab service port rule, observe the symptom and use a layered diagnosis rather than opening all ports.
prove: Explain every route and allowed inbound connection.
The instance uses a scoped role rather than an embedded cloud key.
Inventory and remove the instance and related billable resources after the lab.
weeks.deliverable: Network diagram, sanitized deployment record and cleanup inventory.
weeks.question: Why can an instance have an address but still be unreachable?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Storage, databases and recovery
weeks.outcome: Choose among object storage, block storage and managed relational databases.
weeks.concept: Durability, availability and recoverability answer different questions.
weeks.focus: S3 access controls and versioning; RDS responsibilities; encryption; backups; connection limits.
build: Store a non-sensitive lab object in a private bucket and verify allowed and denied access.
Compare self-managed PostgreSQL with RDS: patching, backups, availability, cost and operational responsibility.
Rehearse database restore locally; execute a short RDS restore lab only if a fresh cost estimate permits it.
weeks.break: Delete a disposable test record and restore into a separate database instead of overwriting the original.
prove: Explain why a read replica is not a backup.
Validate restored rows and application behavior.
Record which AWS behaviors you executed and which you only designed.
weeks.deliverable: Storage decision record and restore report with measured recovery time.
weeks.question: What failures survive replication and therefore require an independent recovery copy?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Gate 4 · review an AWS design
weeks.outcome: Defend a simple AWS architecture against reliability, security and cost requirements.
weeks.concept: Architecture quality is about meeting requirements with understood tradeoffs, not maximizing the number of services.
weeks.focus: Availability zones, load balancing, health checks, blast radius, operating cost and shared responsibility.
build: Design a learning-sized deployment and a separate multi-AZ production proposal.
Document a single-instance failure, database failure and credential leak response.
Estimate both designs using current provider pricing, including load balancers, NAT, logs, storage, backups, IP addresses and egress.
weeks.break: Tabletop an availability-zone failure: identify every dependency that remains a single point of failure.
prove: Your diagram distinguishes implemented from proposed components.
Every major design choice has a requirement and a cost consequence.
Cloud resources are cleaned up and billing is checked again after reporting delay.
weeks.deliverable: AWS design review, cost model and a list of unproven assumptions.
weeks.question: Would two web replicas help if both depend on one unavailable database?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Make infrastructure changes reviewable
weeks.outcome: Use Terraform's configuration, plan, state and apply workflow deliberately.
weeks.concept: Terraform compares desired configuration, recorded state and provider observations. State is not just a disposable cache.
weeks.focus: Providers, resources, data sources, dependencies, outputs, state and replacement.
build: Start with a local-provider exercise, then describe one small AWS resource already understood from weeks 13–16.
Run formatting and validation; inspect a saved plan and explain creates, updates and replacements.
Commit configuration and the provider lock file; keep state, plans and secrets out of public Git.
weeks.break: Change an attribute that forces replacement in a disposable resource. Predict the consequence before applying.
prove: You can read a plan without treating it as a yes/no prompt.
A second plan after convergence has no unexpected changes.
You explain why state can contain sensitive values even when output is marked sensitive.
weeks.deliverable: Small Terraform root module and annotated plan review.
weeks.question: What evidence would make you stop before applying a plan?
weeks.cost: Local first; AWS resource only within explicit lab budget

weeks.title: State, modules and environment boundaries
weeks.outcome: Separate environments and design small modules with stable interfaces.
weeks.concept: A reusable module hides repetition, not operational responsibility.
weeks.focus: Remote state, locking, versioning, variable validation, outputs and state ownership.
build: Move the cloud lab to an access-controlled remote backend with encryption, versioning and supported locking.
Create one small network or service module with documented inputs and outputs.
Separate development and staging state and credentials; document the backend bootstrap and recovery procedure.
weeks.break: Attempt a second operation while the first holds a lab state lock; observe protection without forcibly unlocking an active writer.
prove: State access is restricted and recoverable.
Module input validation rejects a bad value.
You explain why workspaces alone do not create a security boundary.
weeks.deliverable: Module README, state design and lock/recovery exercise.
weeks.question: Who can read state, and what authority or secrets could that reveal?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Test drift, assumptions and changes
weeks.outcome: Catch invalid infrastructure designs and distinguish drift from intended change.
weeks.concept: Syntax validity does not prove network reachability, access control or recoverability.
weeks.focus: Plan assertions, mocked providers, apply tests, drift detection, import and moved resources.
build: Add tests for variable constraints and planned properties using terraform test.
Keep mocked/plan tests separate from apply tests that create real resources and incur cost.
Make one manual lab change, detect the drift and decide whether to restore configuration or adopt the change.
weeks.break: Propose world-open administrative ingress in a lab configuration and make an assertion or policy fail before apply.
prove: A deliberate unsafe change is rejected by an automated check.
Live tests clean up and are verified against the provider inventory.
You can explain a resource move without destroying it.
weeks.deliverable: Terraform test suite, drift report and lifecycle notes.
weeks.question: Which assertions can a mocked provider never prove?
weeks.cost: Mocked tests local; explicitly gated live tests may cost money

weeks.title: Gate 5 · deliver infrastructure through GitLab
weeks.outcome: Plan in a merge request and apply a reviewed change with scoped cloud identity.
weeks.concept: Infrastructure delivery needs authorization, serialization and evidence tied to the exact change.
weeks.focus: OIDC, narrow role trust, saved plans, protected execution and state isolation.
build: Configure GitLab ID-token federation to AWS for your exact project and intended deployment ref.
Run format, validate and tests before a protected plan/apply workflow; limit plan artifact access and retention.
Recreate the small AWS environment from configuration and produce cleanup evidence.
weeks.break: Try the role from the wrong ref or audience and verify denial; do not print the token.
prove: The applied change is tied to the reviewed commit and plan.
Untrusted merge requests cannot obtain deployment authority.
Concurrent writers are serialized and cloud resources can be reconstructed.
weeks.deliverable: Cloud-IaC pipeline with positive and negative identity tests.
weeks.question: What happens if configuration or state changes between planning and applying?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Configure machines consistently
weeks.outcome: Use Ansible inventories, modules and roles to configure your Linux service.
weeks.concept: Terraform owns cloud resources; Ansible configures hosts. Define ownership so two systems do not fight over the same property.
weeks.focus: SSH, inventory, facts, modules, privilege escalation, templates and handlers.
build: Use two disposable Linux VMs or one VM plus an explicit second-host design.
Write a role to create a service user, install prerequisites, render configuration and manage Taskboard's service.
Use handlers so a service restarts when its configuration changes, not after every task.
weeks.break: Introduce an incorrect inventory host or service configuration value and diagnose the failing task.
prove: Host-specific values live in inventory variables rather than duplicated playbooks.
A second normal run is unchanged unless a documented task intentionally varies.
You can explain each privileged action.
weeks.deliverable: Ansible role, example inventory and ownership decision record.
weeks.question: Why prefer a purpose-built package or service module over an unconditional shell command?
weeks.cost: Local VMs

weeks.title: Idempotency, secrets and verification
weeks.outcome: Demonstrate that configuration is repeatable and secret exposure is controlled.
weeks.concept: Check mode predicts changes where supported; it does not substitute for executing and verifying a real configuration.
weeks.focus: Check/diff modes, linting, encrypted data, key separation and post-configuration assertions.
build: Lint the role and compare check/diff output with an actual run on a disposable host.
Keep secret decryption keys outside Git and log output; use encrypted configuration only where its delivery model is understood.
Assert that the expected port, user, file permissions and service endpoint are correct after configuration.
weeks.break: Apply a wrong file owner or mode in the lab and ensure a post-configuration assertion catches it.
prove: Two consecutive runs demonstrate intended idempotency.
Secrets are absent from repository history, diffs and normal logs.
Unsupported check-mode behavior is documented rather than mistaken for success.
weeks.deliverable: Configuration verification report and secret-access diagram.
weeks.question: Who can decrypt this file, and how would you rotate that access?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Harden and patch with evidence
weeks.outcome: Improve a host baseline without breaking legitimate service behavior.
weeks.concept: A scanner finding is a lead for investigation. Hardening needs threat context, validation and recovery.
weeks.focus: Patch management, service permissions, SSH access, firewall policy, audit evidence and exceptions.
build: Audit the disposable VM with Lynis and classify findings by applicability and risk.
Implement three justified changes through Ansible, with before/after evidence.
Patch a dependency or package, then run service and system tests and rehearse recovery.
weeks.break: Introduce a restrictive lab permission that blocks the service. Restore only the needed access.
prove: Every accepted finding has a reason and a verification step.
Hardening changes preserve required user behavior.
You retain an access and rollback path during configuration changes.
weeks.deliverable: Hardening change record, exception register and verified patch procedure.
weeks.question: When can a higher audit score make a real system less operable?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Gate 6 · rebuild the VM platform
weeks.outcome: Provision, configure, deploy, restore and explain one complete environment.
weeks.concept: Repeatability is demonstrated by a rebuild, not by how much infrastructure code exists.
weeks.focus: Ownership boundaries, bootstrap, external dependencies and handoff.
build: Rebuild from Terraform plus Ansible and deploy a GitLab-tested artifact.
Restore test data and run the unit, integration and system test evidence appropriate to the release.
Have another person follow the runbook, or simulate a fresh-operator review using only the written instructions.
weeks.break: Remove a disposable host and replace it; separately simulate a bad configuration rollout.
prove: The replacement is created without undocumented console steps.
Recovery time is measured and remaining manual steps are explicit.
The system can be cleaned up without deleting unrelated resources.
weeks.deliverable: First portfolio project: reproducible VM platform with recovery proof.
weeks.question: Which part of the environment cannot yet be reconstructed, and what would close that gap?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Learn reconciliation on a local cluster
weeks.outcome: Explain what the API server, scheduler, controllers, kubelet and container runtime do.
weeks.concept: Kubernetes continuously reconciles declared objects with observed reality. A running Pod is an outcome of several cooperating components.
weeks.focus: Cluster architecture, namespaces, manifests, Pods, Deployments and kubectl observation.
build: Create a local kind cluster and record compatible tool versions.
Deploy the known Taskboard image with a Deployment and inspect objects, events and logs.
Delete a disposable Pod and observe replacement through the owning Deployment and ReplicaSet.
weeks.break: Use a nonexistent image tag and diagnose ImagePullBackOff from events.
prove: You explain why editing a Pod manually is not a durable deployment change.
You can identify an object's owner and desired replica count.
Your manifests are versioned and reproducible.
weeks.deliverable: Cluster architecture explanation and first Kubernetes manifests.
weeks.question: What does Kubernetes know about your application's business correctness?
weeks.cost: Local; a multi-node kind cluster is not multi-machine availability

weeks.title: Traffic, probes and safe rollout
weeks.outcome: Route requests to ready application instances and handle startup and shutdown correctly.
weeks.concept: Readiness controls traffic eligibility; liveness can trigger restart; startup probes protect slow initialization.
weeks.focus: Services, selectors, EndpointSlices, DNS, probes, rollout status and graceful termination.
build: Expose Taskboard internally through a Service and test service discovery.
Add appropriate startup/readiness/liveness checks; do not make liveness depend on a transient database outage.
Roll out a new digest while sending a small stream of local requests; record failures and termination behavior.
weeks.break: Use a wrong Service selector, then a failing readiness check. Diagnose the two failures separately.
prove: Unready instances stop receiving normal Service traffic.
A slow start is not mistaken for a permanently dead process.
You can explain and measure a rollout rather than only observing Running status.
weeks.deliverable: Probe design, traffic-path diagram and rollout report.
weeks.question: How could a poorly designed liveness probe turn a database outage into a restart storm?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Configuration and workload security
weeks.outcome: Limit workload permissions and verify network isolation.
weeks.concept: Namespaces organize objects; access control and network policy enforce specific boundaries.
weeks.focus: ConfigMaps, Secrets, RBAC, service accounts, security contexts, Pod Security and NetworkPolicy.
build: Run the app without privileged mode, with minimal capabilities and an explicit service account.
Add narrowly scoped RBAC and demonstrate an allowed and denied action.
Use a NetworkPolicy-capable CNI in the lab; allow app-to-database traffic and deny an unrelated test workload.
weeks.break: Apply a policy missing the required DNS or database egress, then use evidence to add only the necessary rule.
prove: Network policy enforcement is tested, not inferred from the existence of YAML.
You explain that base64 encoding is not secret encryption.
The app cannot perform an unnecessary Kubernetes API action.
weeks.deliverable: Workload threat model, RBAC checks and network-policy tests.
weeks.question: What can a compromised app do with its mounted service-account token?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Gate 7 · diagnose Kubernetes failures
weeks.outcome: Use symptoms and evidence to distinguish scheduling, startup, traffic and application failures.
weeks.concept: Events, logs, object state and actual requests answer different questions. Read them in a hypothesis-driven order.
weeks.focus: Pending, CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, selectors and dependency failures.
build: Create a troubleshooting decision tree with commands and expected observations.
Practise image, configuration, readiness, selector and resource-request failures one at a time.
Use Headlamp or Freelens only after diagnosing the same symptom with kubectl.
weeks.break: Have a peer choose one fault without naming it, or randomize one of your previously prepared lab faults.
prove: You preserve evidence before changing the deployment.
The diagnosis explains the observed failure and the regression check.
You can repeat the diagnosis without relying on a dashboard or AI explanation.
weeks.deliverable: Five incident notes and one independently diagnosed fault.
weeks.question: Which observation would falsify your leading hypothesis?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Understand state and operators
weeks.outcome: Explain Kubernetes storage and the operational cost of running a database in a cluster.
weeks.concept: Scheduling a database is easier than operating its storage, replication, backups, upgrades and recovery.
weeks.focus: PersistentVolumes, claims, StorageClasses, StatefulSets, operators and backup boundaries.
build: Run a small disposable PostgreSQL workload with a persistent claim and observe restart behavior.
Read CloudNativePG's current backup/plugin and recovery guidance and compare it with a managed database.
Prepare a restore lab with separate source and target data; install the operator only if local resources permit.
weeks.break: Use an unavailable StorageClass or unsatisfied claim and diagnose why the workload remains pending.
prove: You distinguish Pod persistence from volume durability and from backups.
You can explain what the operator owns.
Your design includes a recovery route when the original cluster is unavailable.
weeks.deliverable: Database placement decision and storage failure record.
weeks.question: Would deleting and recreating a Pod help if the volume itself is corrupt?
weeks.cost: Local; operator exercise can be deferred if hardware is constrained

weeks.title: Measure capacity before scaling
weeks.outcome: Set resource requests and limits from observed behavior and reason about autoscaling.
weeks.concept: Adding replicas can move a bottleneck to the database or another dependency.
weeks.focus: CPU requests, throttling, memory limits, OOM, metrics availability and HPA behavior.
build: Measure CPU, memory, latency and error rate under a repeatable local workload.
Choose starting requests/limits with a written rationale.
Configure an HPA with its required metrics source; observe scale-out and scale-in while tracking database connections.
weeks.break: Set an intentionally small memory limit in the disposable lab and distinguish an OOM termination from a probe failure.
prove: The load report includes saturation and tail latency, not only average response time.
You explain why the HPA did or did not react.
Scaling limits respect downstream capacity and budget.
weeks.deliverable: Capacity model with measured assumptions and autoscaling evidence.
weeks.question: How can more application replicas make database availability worse?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: GitLab CI plus Argo CD
weeks.outcome: Separate building an artifact from reconciling a cluster to approved configuration.
weeks.concept: GitOps uses versioned desired state and a controller to reconcile it; it does not eliminate authorization or recovery design.
weeks.focus: Image digests, environment configuration, reconciliation, drift, sync and secret handling.
build: Let GitLab build/test/publish; let Argo CD reconcile a separate environment configuration path or repository.
Deploy podinfo first to isolate platform learning, then Taskboard.
Use SOPS only with an explicitly understood decryption integration; otherwise keep secrets external to plaintext Git.
weeks.break: Make an intentional manual lab change and observe drift and the configured reconciliation policy.
prove: The source commit, image digest and deployed revision can be traced.
No two controllers compete to own the same field.
A revert restores desired state subject to schema compatibility.
weeks.deliverable: GitOps architecture and drift/recovery recording.
weeks.question: What prevents a malicious configuration change from being faithfully reconciled?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Gate 8 · release and recover on Kubernetes
weeks.outcome: Operate your service through a controlled update, failure and recovery.
weeks.concept: Availability must be measured during change; a final green dashboard does not reveal an outage during rollout.
weeks.focus: Rolling updates, disruption budgets, replica placement, rollout failure and rollback.
build: Set rollout behavior based on measured startup and shutdown characteristics.
Run system tests and a small request stream while deploying a new version.
Document what a PodDisruptionBudget covers and what local kind cannot prove about real node or zone loss.
weeks.break: Release an image that never becomes ready, then recover through the source of truth.
prove: The rollout failure is detected and its impact measured.
The last working image and configuration are recoverable.
You explain database compatibility and remaining single points of failure.
weeks.deliverable: Second portfolio project: Kubernetes delivery and recovery evidence.
weeks.question: What failure would your disruption budget not protect you from?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Measure the user experience
weeks.outcome: Instrument useful metrics and create a small actionable dashboard.
weeks.concept: A metric should support a decision or diagnosis; collecting more data is not automatically better observability.
weeks.focus: Request rate, errors, duration, saturation, labels, histograms and external probes.
build: Expose request count, error count and duration histogram metrics.
Build a Prometheus/Grafana view of request rate, error ratio, latency and resource saturation.
Add Gatus or a simple external probe that exercises a meaningful service endpoint.
weeks.break: Cause an endpoint failure while the process remains running and compare process health with user-visible availability.
prove: Every dashboard panel answers a named question.
Labels avoid unbounded user IDs, task IDs or raw URLs.
The external check detects a failure the process check misses.
weeks.deliverable: Dashboard definition and a metric design note.
weeks.question: Why can a low overall error rate hide a completely broken endpoint?
weeks.cost: Local; choose one metrics stack

weeks.title: Connect logs and traces
weeks.outcome: Follow a slow request across service and database boundaries.
weeks.concept: Metrics describe aggregate behavior, logs capture events, and traces connect operations for a request.
weeks.focus: Trace context, spans, structured logs, sampling, sensitive data and retention.
build: Instrument Taskboard with OpenTelemetry and carry a request/trace identifier through logs.
Choose one local trace backend; inspect SigNoz as an option rather than adding multiple stacks.
Create a controlled slow database call and correlate latency metrics, logs and a trace.
weeks.break: Drop trace context at one boundary and show how it breaks the diagnostic story.
prove: You identify the slow operation from a trace and confirm it independently.
Logs omit credentials and unnecessary personal data.
Retention and sampling decisions have an explicit cost and privacy rationale.
weeks.deliverable: One end-to-end trace investigation and telemetry policy.
weeks.question: What evidence is lost when a request is not sampled?
weeks.cost: Local; use a lighter backend if hardware is constrained

weeks.title: Define SLOs and useful alerts
weeks.outcome: Turn service expectations into measurable targets and release decisions.
weeks.concept: An SLO is a target for a defined indicator over a window. An error budget makes the tolerance for failure explicit.
weeks.focus: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, burn rate, low-traffic caveats and alert actions.
build: Define eligible requests, good requests, measurement location and a rolling window.
Use a lab availability target such as 99.5% and a separate latency target; label both as chosen exercises.
Write an alert with a runbook and evaluate it using synthetic fault data or a controlled outage.
weeks.break: Create a rapid burst of errors and compare detection with a slow sustained degradation.
prove: You can calculate the remaining request-based error budget.
An alert identifies a user-impacting symptom and a next action.
You do not infer a 30-day SLO from a ten-minute successful test.
weeks.deliverable: SLO document, budget calculation and alert evaluation.
weeks.question: When should reliability evidence delay a feature release?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Gate 9 · run an incident
weeks.outcome: Detect, mitigate, communicate and learn from a service failure.
weeks.concept: During an incident, restore useful service while preserving evidence; root-cause analysis can continue after mitigation.
weeks.focus: Incident roles, timeline, hypotheses, mitigation, status communication and blameless follow-up.
build: Prepare a short incident protocol and a symptom-based runbook.
Run a timed game day with one controlled dependency or deployment failure.
Write an incident report with impact, timeline, contributing conditions, detection gaps and owned follow-up actions.
weeks.break: Choose a fault the dashboards do not immediately identify; observe whether the runbook narrows it safely.
prove: Detection and recovery times are measured from explicit events.
Updates describe known impact and uncertainty without invented certainty.
At least one prevention or detection improvement is implemented and retested.
weeks.deliverable: Incident dossier and improved runbook.
weeks.question: What made this error possible or hard to detect beyond the individual who triggered it?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Translate identity, not just names
weeks.outcome: Understand Google Cloud projects, IAM, service accounts and billing.
weeks.concept: Similar service categories do not imply identical identity, networking or organizational behavior.
weeks.focus: Organization/folder/project hierarchy, IAM bindings, service identities, quotas and budgets.
build: Create a comparison of AWS accounts/roles and GCP projects/service accounts with the differences stated.
Design an isolated learning project and budget notifications before paid usage.
Use a limited identity and inspect permissions on a harmless resource.
weeks.break: Test a deliberately denied read or write and locate the relevant permission boundary.
prove: You can identify the active project and identity.
You avoid exported long-lived service-account keys in the planned delivery workflow.
You explain why budget alerts do not cap spending.
weeks.deliverable: GCP identity map and AWS/GCP comparison table.
weeks.question: What can go wrong if a command uses the correct account but the wrong project?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Networking, compute and storage on GCP
weeks.outcome: Deploy a small familiar workload while examining cloud differences.
weeks.concept: Portability belongs at chosen interfaces; cloud-specific capabilities still require explicit design.
weeks.focus: VPC scope, regional subnets, firewall policy, instance identity, storage permissions and logs.
build: Draw a GCP traffic path and compare its resource scope with AWS.

Deploy the same Taskboard image on a short-lived Compute Engine VM if budget permits. Preserve private/tunneled access unless the established public authentication and authorization model has been implemented and verified.
Test private object access with a scoped identity and document cleanup.
weeks.break: Use an incorrect service identity or firewall rule in the lab and diagnose without granting broad access.
prove: The app image remains unchanged while cloud configuration differs.
Allowed and denied access are both demonstrated.
The inventory includes persistent disks, addresses and storage after VM removal.
weeks.deliverable: GCP deployment record and portability decision.
weeks.question: Which parts of the AWS network design cannot be copied mechanically?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Terraform and GitLab federation on GCP
weeks.outcome: Deliver a small GCP workload with short-lived pipeline identity.
weeks.concept: Workload identity federation connects an external identity to narrowly authorized cloud actions.
weeks.focus: Workload identity pools/providers, attribute conditions, impersonation, remote state and serverless constraints.
build: Create Terraform configuration for the chosen small GCP deployment and isolate its state from AWS.
Configure GitLab federation scoped to the intended project/ref and deploy without a downloaded service-account key.

Evaluate Cloud Run using podinfo or a stateless Taskboard variant; require authenticated invocation for the lab and document external state, concurrency and scaling constraints. Do not publicly expose Taskboard's teaching authentication mechanism.
weeks.break: Change an audience or attribute condition in the lab and verify that incorrect identity is rejected.
prove: The deploy job obtains short-lived authority only for the intended scope.
No persistent application data relies on a container's ephemeral filesystem.
The exact deployed image digest is traceable to test results.
weeks.deliverable: GCP delivery pipeline and federation verification.
weeks.question: Why is identity federation still dangerous if the authorized role is too broad?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Gate 10 · compare managed platforms
weeks.outcome: Choose between VMs, managed containers and managed Kubernetes for stated needs.
weeks.concept: Operational simplicity is an architectural advantage when it meets the requirements.
weeks.focus: Managed control planes, workload identity, upgrades, networking, availability and total operating cost.
build: Compare EC2/Compute Engine, a managed container service, EKS and GKE against Taskboard's requirements.
Choose one managed Kubernetes lab, EKS or GKE, for a short execution if budget permits; keep the other a documented comparison.
Deploy the known manifests, test identity and traffic, then remove the cluster and dependent resources.
weeks.break: Tabletop loss of a node and an unavailable control plane; separate provider and customer responsibilities.
prove: You can justify choosing a simpler platform when Kubernetes adds unnecessary work.
The comparison includes ongoing operations and cost, not only initial deployment.
Executed and design-only capabilities are clearly labeled.
weeks.deliverable: Cloud platform decision and optional managed-cluster evidence.
weeks.question: Which responsibilities remain yours even with a managed control plane?
weeks.cost: Free local core practice; optional provider execution may incur charges and has separate evidence.

weeks.title: Secure the software supply chain
weeks.outcome: Trace source, dependencies, build identity and artifact integrity.
weeks.concept: A vulnerability scan is one signal; provenance and authorization answer different trust questions.
weeks.focus: SBOMs, image scanning, signatures, provenance, dependency updates and exception expiry.
build: Generate an SBOM and scan the application image using one selected tool.
Triage findings by exposure, exploitability, fix availability and operational context; assign time-limited exceptions.
Sign or attest the artifact and verify the expected identity and digest before a lab deployment.
weeks.break: Try to deploy an unexpected digest or untrusted signing identity and make the release check reject it.
prove: The signature is verified against an identity policy, not merely present.
A critical finding has a documented fix or explicit scoped exception.
You can trace a running digest back to source and build evidence.
weeks.deliverable: Supply-chain evidence bundle and update procedure.
weeks.question: What does a valid signature prove, and what does it leave unproven?
weeks.cost: Local/CI; verify chosen tool and hosted service terms

weeks.title: Migrate and recover data safely
weeks.outcome: Change schemas compatibly and prove restoration of meaningful data.
weeks.concept: Deployment rollback and data rollback are different operations with different risks.
weeks.focus: Expand/contract migrations, old/new app compatibility, backup retention, WAL and point-in-time recovery.
build: Add an optional field using an expand/contract sequence; test old and new application versions against the expanded schema.
Schedule a local backup and restore to a separate destination using PostgreSQL tooling or one audited backup tool.
If practising PITR, verify the exact selected tool/version supports the required backup and WAL recovery path.
weeks.break: Delete a disposable record at a known time and recover the intended data without overwriting the source environment.
prove: A migration test catches incompatible schema changes.
The restored app passes system tests and content checks.
Measured data loss and recovery time are compared with your chosen RPO/RTO.
weeks.deliverable: Migration compatibility matrix and restore drill report.
weeks.question: How would you know a successful-looking backup is actually usable?
weeks.cost: Local; backups and retention in cloud are billable

weeks.title: Scale with bottlenecks in mind
weeks.outcome: Improve measured performance while controlling overload and consistency.
weeks.concept: Queues absorb bursts only while capacity and retention are sufficient; retries can multiply load.
weeks.focus: Indexes, connection pools, bounded queues, backpressure, timeouts, retries with jitter and idempotency.
build: Use profiling or query evidence to identify one bottleneck and improve it.
Add an optional background task with an idempotency key only if it solves a stated requirement.
Set bounded timeouts and retry behavior; compare baseline and changed throughput, p95/p99, errors and resource cost.
weeks.break: Slow a dependency or deliver the same background message twice. Observe retry amplification or duplicate work and fix it.
prove: The improvement is supported by comparable before/after conditions.
If a background task was added, duplicate delivery cannot silently double-apply the chosen operation; otherwise document this extension as not implemented.
The service degrades predictably when downstream capacity is exhausted.
weeks.deliverable: Performance investigation and overload behavior report.
weeks.question: When is rejecting work quickly safer than accepting it into an ever-growing queue?
weeks.cost: Local controlled load

weeks.title: Gate 11 · recovery game day
weeks.outcome: Recover both service and data under explicit constraints.
weeks.concept: High availability reduces some interruptions; disaster recovery prepares for loss of the normal operating environment.
weeks.focus: RTO, RPO, dependencies, credential recovery, backup access and communication.
build: Set achievable lab targets, for example RTO 30 minutes and RPO 24 hours for daily logical backups.
Simulate losing a disposable environment; rebuild it and restore into a fresh target.
Audit whether backups, decryption keys, configuration and runbooks survive the same failure boundary.
weeks.break: Make the normal cluster unavailable while preserving a separate lab backup; restore without depending on the old cluster.
prove: Measured recovery and data loss meet your stated lab targets or produce a remediation plan.
Restoration passes meaningful system checks.
A failed drill is reported accurately rather than marked complete.
weeks.deliverable: Disaster-recovery report and revised dependencies map.
weeks.question: Which shared dependency could make both your primary system and recovery plan fail?
weeks.cost: Local default; any cloud reconstruction has a fresh cost estimate

weeks.title: Kubernetes internals, deliberately
weeks.outcome: Understand certificate trust, component communication and control-plane state.
weeks.concept: A managed cluster hides implementation work, not the need to understand its failure modes.
weeks.focus: PKI, kubeconfigs, API authorization, etcd, control-plane components and node registration.
build: Read the current Kubernetes The Hard Way prerequisites and choose compatible disposable VMs.
Trace component-to-component trust and produce a certificate/identity map.
Complete the first bounded set of current upstream steps; annotate what every credential and configuration file permits.
weeks.break: Inspect a deliberately wrong lab endpoint or expired test certificate without changing real cluster credentials.
prove: You can explain why each component needs its identity.
You understand the difference between authentication and authorization.
You record upstream commit/version and mark unfinished steps explicitly.
weeks.deliverable: Kubernetes trust map and first internals lab notes.
weeks.question: Why is copying an administrator kubeconfig to every machine a poor design?
weeks.cost: Local VMs; selected reading-only path if hardware cannot support the lab

weeks.title: Upgrades and component failures
weeks.outcome: Plan a cluster upgrade and diagnose a bounded component failure.
weeks.concept: The cluster is itself a system to operate, including version compatibility, certificates, storage and recovery.
weeks.focus: Version skew, backup scope, certificate lifecycle, draining and upgrade validation.
build: Complete the chosen Hard Way scope or document a component-focused alternative.
Read current version-skew guidance and plan an upgrade of a disposable cluster.
Exercise prechecks, a bounded update, postchecks and an explicit recovery decision; distinguish workload backup from etcd backup.
weeks.break: Stop a lab worker service or misconfigure a component endpoint and trace symptoms back to the component.
prove: The upgrade plan respects currently supported version skew.
You identify which failures stop new scheduling versus existing traffic.
You can explain what restoring etcd does and does not restore.
weeks.deliverable: Upgrade runbook and component failure investigation.
weeks.question: Which application data is absent from an etcd snapshot?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Make a paved path for another developer
weeks.outcome: Turn your working conventions into a small usable service template.
weeks.concept: Platform engineering reduces repeated cognitive work while retaining clear escape hatches and ownership.
weeks.focus: Service templates, documentation, defaults, developer feedback and support boundaries.
build: Create a template with health endpoints, tests, CI, configuration conventions and a runbook.
Provide understandable commands for development, testing and deployment.
Evaluate Semaphore or another audited platform only against a specific usability problem; keep the default workflow small.
weeks.break: Give the template an invalid configuration and improve the resulting error message and documentation.
prove: A new user can start the example with documented prerequisites.
Defaults limit privilege and secret exposure.
The template describes what its maintainers own and what application owners own.
weeks.deliverable: Service template v1 and developer onboarding notes.
weeks.question: Does this abstraction remove work or merely hide failure modes?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Gate 12 · independent engineering review
weeks.outcome: Demonstrate transferable judgment beyond a rehearsed tutorial.
weeks.concept: Competence includes explaining when not to use a tool and recovering when the tutorial's assumptions fail.
weeks.focus: Design critique, practical diagnosis, communication and identifying gaps.
build: Answer a selected set of unseen Linux, cloud, Kubernetes, Terraform and SRE questions without notes, then verify against current docs.
Perform two previously unseen local fault investigations.
Review a proposed overcomplicated architecture and simplify it with explicit tradeoffs.
weeks.break: Use an unfamiliar combination of two known faults, preserving an escape route.
prove: Each incorrect explanation becomes a concrete remedial exercise.
You separate measured facts from hypotheses.
You can explain the system to both a developer and a non-technical stakeholder.
weeks.deliverable: Competency scorecard and capstone gap list.
weeks.question: Which skills are demonstrated independently, and which still depend on a guide?
weeks.cost: Local

weeks.title: Specify a service worth operating
weeks.outcome: Translate a small product need into testable operational requirements.
weeks.concept: Production readiness is relative to users, risk, workload and operating constraints.
weeks.focus: Requirements, threat model, capacity assumptions, SLO, cost ceiling and ownership.
build: Write a Taskboard service brief with users, data sensitivity, expected traffic and failure consequences.
Choose one primary deployment platform; retain the second cloud as a tested portability exercise rather than mandatory active-active complexity.
Define acceptance tests, recovery targets, monitoring, update policy and architecture decisions before building.
weeks.break: Challenge one assumption: tenfold traffic, loss of a zone, leaked credential or incompatible schema change.
prove: Every major control traces to a requirement or threat.
Targets include measurement method and test conditions.
The design fits a stated operating budget.
weeks.deliverable: Capstone service brief, threat model and acceptance contract.
weeks.question: What would make this architecture insufficient for a real customer?
weeks.cost: Planning; paid execution only after estimating the chosen design

weeks.title: Build and deliver the complete system
weeks.outcome: Integrate application, infrastructure, delivery, security and observability into a reproducible release.
weeks.concept: The final project should demonstrate a coherent operating system of practices, not a collection of tool screenshots.
weeks.focus: Infrastructure/configuration ownership, tested artifacts, identity, restore and documentation.
build: Rebuild the chosen platform from code and deploy the exact tested image.
Run unit, real integration and system tests plus infrastructure and security checks.
Attach telemetry, release evidence, backup verification and current cost inventory.
weeks.break: Attempt a release with one deliberately failed acceptance condition and verify the release decision rejects it.
prove: No critical operational step exists only in your memory.
Source, artifact, configuration and deployment revisions are traceable.
The release can be reproduced from a clean environment.
weeks.deliverable: Capstone release candidate and evidence index.
weeks.question: Which part of the delivery path has the broadest authority, and how is it constrained?
weeks.cost: Local valid; cloud claims require real cloud evidence

weeks.title: Break it under review
weeks.outcome: Demonstrate recovery, diagnosis and communication under realistic lab pressure.
weeks.concept: Failure drills test the system and its operating procedures together.
weeks.focus: Blind incidents, restore validation, load behavior, rollback and follow-up work.
build: Run one deployment failure, one dependency/network failure and one data-recovery scenario.
Perform a controlled load test at the declared workload and compare against latency/error targets.
Produce one incident report with a prioritized remediation backlog and retest the highest-risk improvement.
weeks.break: Let a reviewer select the fault, or use a randomized prepared scenario and avoid inspecting the fault source before diagnosis.
prove: Recovery and performance claims have timestamped evidence and stated limits.
No lost or duplicate user operation is hidden by a green infrastructure dashboard.
The operator can communicate impact while continuing diagnosis.
weeks.deliverable: Final game-day and performance dossier.
weeks.question: What failed in your process even if the service was eventually restored?
weeks.cost: Local default; controlled budgeted cloud session if selected

weeks.title: Gate 13 · hand it to another engineer
weeks.outcome: Present a defensible portfolio and a clear map of your next learning needs.
weeks.concept: Strong engineering makes systems understandable and maintainable by people other than their original author.
weeks.focus: Handoff, architecture explanation, operational readiness, honest claims and continued practice.
build: Have another person rebuild, deploy and recover from your documentation; if unavailable, do a fresh-environment self-review and label it accordingly.
Score the capstone using the readiness rubric, resolving critical failures.
Write a concise portfolio narrative: problem, constraints, choices, evidence, incidents, tradeoffs and remaining limitations.
weeks.break: Remove your informal assistance from the handoff and identify every point where the documentation is insufficient.
prove: All mandatory gates have evidence or are explicitly incomplete.
The portfolio does not claim seniority or production reliability from lab duration alone.
You have a specific next-quarter plan based on demonstrated weaknesses.
weeks.deliverable: Portfolio, handoff package, final scorecard and next-quarter improvement plan.
weeks.question: Would a teammate trust you to explain the risk of a change and help recover when it fails?
weeks.cost: No additional infrastructure required
